# The New Philanthropy and the Legitimation Machine {#sec-5-05}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Open Era · 2010–2020
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does a modern monopolist make power invisible?

**The answer.** By giving it away on his own terms. Modern monopoly legitimacy
is purchased through philanthropy, university endowment, and public-benefit
storytelling — structures that convert a fortune into disinterested authority
while leaving control with the donor. It is the Medici playbook from Act I ch.
7, executed with better tax treatment.

**The mechanism.** Elite network reproduction and the manufacture of legitimacy,
and the book's most direct historical rhyme. Leland Stanford endowed a
university and the university certified the class it produced. The limited-
liability company structured as a philanthropic vehicle does the same work
without even the constraints of a foundation.

**The key fact.** The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative was structured as a limited
liability company rather than a foundation, which permits political spending and
investment alongside grantmaking and carries no payout requirement. The form is
the argument.

**The human anchor.** A building with a name on it. The chapter should return to
Act I's donor altarpiece: the same transaction, the same permanence, the same
eye-level placement.

**Excluded voices.** The public, which forgoes tax revenue and receives no vote
over how the resulting funds are deployed, and the fields and regions
philanthropic priorities do not favour. Also grant recipients whose independence
is constrained by dependence.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that philanthropy operates as a legitimacy
instrument by showing the same donors endowing the institutions that credential
their own class.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Six hundred years after a Florentine banker had his face painted into an
altarpiece, the same transaction is conducted with a building and a tax
deduction. The chapter opens by returning to Act I and then examines the
instruments.

Modern legitimacy is purchased through philanthropy, university endowment, and
public-benefit storytelling, and the structures matter more than the sums. A
private foundation carries a minimum payout requirement and disclosure
obligations. A donor-advised fund carries neither and can hold assets
indefinitely. And the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative was constituted as a limited
liability company rather than a foundation, which permits political spending and
for-profit investment alongside grantmaking and imposes no payout requirement at
all. The chapter states the defensible reasons for that choice and then examines
its effects, because the form is the argument.

University endowment remains the core move, and the book has already documented
it twice: Leland Stanford in 1885, and Phil Knight with the management centre
and the scholars programme. The institution that certifies the elite is funded
by the elite it certifies, and the names over the doors are the receipt.

The Thiel Fellowship is the chapter's sharpest case, because it appears to
contradict the thesis by paying students to leave university. What it actually
does is substitute one gatekeeper for another — a smaller, less accountable, and
more personal one — which strengthens the argument rather than weakening it.

Venture capital as ideological publisher belongs here too: funding the narrative
about what technology is for, alongside the companies.

What all of it buys is regulatory forbearance, press access, and the presumption
of good faith.

The public forgoes tax revenue and receives no vote over how the resulting funds
are deployed, and grantees dependent on continued funding are not free to say
so. The most efficient route to being untouchable is to become indispensable to
the institutions that decide who is respectable.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}

9. **Landing.** The most efficient way to become untouchable is to become
   indispensable to the institutions that decide who is respectable. Stanford
   learned it in 1885; the Valley relearned it with better accountants.

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does a modern monopolist make power invisible?
:::

Six hundred years after a Florentine banker had his likeness painted into an
altarpiece he had commissioned, the same transaction is conducted with a
building and a tax deduction.

Act I chapter 7 described the Medici method: fund the institution you wish to
control, then staff it, then become it, and commission the culture that explains
why you deserve to. This chapter is that method in its current instruments, and
the instruments are the interesting part.

## Three vehicles

The choice of legal form determines almost everything, and the differences are
technical in a way that rewards attention.

A **private foundation** receives a charitable deduction on contribution, pays a
small excise tax, must distribute a minimum percentage of its assets annually,
and files a public return disclosing its grants and investments. It cannot make
political contributions.

A **donor-advised fund** receives the deduction on contribution, has no payout
requirement at all, and discloses nothing about the individual donor's
recommendations. Money can sit in one indefinitely while the deduction has
already been taken.

A **limited liability company** receives no deduction on formation, because
nothing has been given away. In exchange it can do anything: make grants, make
investments for profit, fund political advocacy, and lobby, with no payout
requirement and no disclosure obligation.

The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, announced in 2015 with a commitment of the great
majority of the founders' Facebook shares, was constituted as an LLC.

The defensible reasons were stated at the time and are real. A foundation cannot
invest in a company developing a technology it wants to see exist, and cannot
fund policy advocacy, and both are legitimate philanthropic strategies. Emerson
Collective, established by Laurene Powell Jobs, took the same form for similar
reasons.

The effect is that a very large pool of capital committed to public purposes
operates with no payout requirement, no grant disclosure, no restriction on
political spending, and no external accountability whatsoever. The commitment is
sincere and the structure is unenforceable, and the donor retains full control
of both the money and the definition of the purpose.

## The university, again

The core move has not changed since 1885, and this book has now documented it
three times in three centuries.

Leland Stanford converted a railroad fortune into a university with a self-
perpetuating board. Phil Knight converted a footwear fortune into a business
school complex and a graduate scholarship programme at the same institution. The
technology fortunes of the present are converting into named buildings,
institutes, and professorships across the same campus and its peers.

The circuit closes on itself. The institution that certifies the elite is funded
by the elite it certified, and each gift both expresses gratitude and increases
the value of the credential the donor holds.

Nothing about this is improper and all of it is self-reinforcing.

## The fellowship that proves the rule

The most interesting case is the one that appears to contradict everything
above.

The Thiel Fellowship, established in 2011, pays young people a substantial sum
on condition that they do not attend university, or that they leave. Its
founder's argument is that higher education has become a credentialling racket
that consumes years and money while teaching conformity, and that talented
people should build things instead.

Much of the critique is accurate, and this book has spent five acts making a
version of it.

But look at what the fellowship actually does. It replaces an institutional
credential — issued by an organisation with published criteria, an admissions
process, and some degree of external scrutiny — with a personal one, awarded by
a small selection committee associated with a single financier, on criteria that
are not published, to a cohort of a couple of dozen people a year.

That is not the abolition of a gatekeeper. It is a smaller, less accountable,
and more concentrated gatekeeper. A fellow's asset is precisely the association:
the signal that this particular network has identified them, which is exactly
the function a Stanford degree performs and which the fellowship exists to
criticise.

The chapter's argument is strengthened rather than embarrassed by the case.
Credentialling is not a feature of universities. It is a function that some
institution will always perform, and the question is only who performs it and
with what accountability.

## Funding the story

The final instrument is the narrative itself, and it is the most direct
descendant of the Medici commission.

Venture firms now operate substantial media and publishing operations: podcasts,
editorial sites, research reports, and campaigns organised around themes. The
most explicit of these is the American Dynamism programme at Andreessen
Horowitz, which frames investment in defence, aerospace, energy, and
manufacturing as a project of national renewal.

That is a coherent thesis and it is also a legitimacy instrument. It supplies an
account in which the firm's investments are a public service, and the account
circulates in a media environment where the firm is also a publisher.

Act I put it this way: cultural production is legitimacy production. The Medici
commissioned altarpieces. A venture partnership commissions a podcast.

## The Giving Pledge and the problem of scale

There is a version of this chapter that treats large-scale philanthropy as
simply good, and the honest objection to it is not about motive.

The Giving Pledge, launched in 2010, is a public commitment by very wealthy
individuals to give the majority of their wealth away. Hundreds have signed. The
sums involved are enormous and a great deal of genuinely valuable work has been
funded with them — in global health above all, where the reduction in deaths
from malaria and from vaccine-preventable disease over the last twenty-five
years is one of the more substantial achievements of the period and was
substantially philanthropically financed.

The chapter records that without qualification, because it is true and because
an argument that cannot acknowledge it is not serious.

The objection is structural. A pledge is not enforceable. Several signatories
are substantially wealthier now than when they signed, because assets have
appreciated faster than they have been given away, which means the commitment
has in practice functioned as a commitment to give away a fortune that keeps
growing.

And the deeper problem is that the scale of these fortunes gives individuals
discretion over public questions on a scale that no democratic mechanism
authorised. When a single foundation's expenditure on a disease exceeds that of
the international agency nominally coordinating the response, the foundation
sets the agenda whatever its intentions, because everyone else's funding depends
on alignment with it.

That is chokepoint control applied to the definition of what counts as a problem
worth solving, and the people affected have no vote.

## What it buys

Legitimacy is not an abstraction and its returns are specific.

It buys regulatory forbearance, because a legislator is slower to attack a
person who funds the hospital wing. It buys press access, because a foundation
with a communications budget shapes what gets covered. It buys the presumption
of good faith in a dispute. And it buys the ability to define problems: a
philanthropy that funds education research substantially determines which
questions about education are asked.

## Who pays

The public forgoes the tax revenue and receives no vote over how the resulting
funds are used.

That is the whole objection and it is sufficient. A charitable deduction is a
public subsidy: the treasury collects less, and the difference is directed
according to the preferences of the donor rather than of the electorate. For
very large fortunes the sums involved are large enough to fund substantial
public programmes.

Grantees, meanwhile, are not free to criticise the hand that funds them, which
constrains the sector's capacity to say anything uncomfortable about the source
of its money. And the fields philanthropic attention does not favour go
unfunded, selected against by preferences nobody voted on.

The most efficient way to become untouchable is to become indispensable to the
institutions that decide who is respectable. Stanford learned that in 1885. The
corridor relearned it with better accountants.
